title: Bigger steps, faster descent?
hook: Bigger steps should reach the bottom of the valley sooner. Try it.

knows: reading a curve on a graph
that a steeper slope means a bigger change

misconception: A bigger step size always gets gradient descent to the minimum faster.
objective: The learner can explain that each step moves (step size × slope), so a step size that is too small crawls, one that is too big overshoots and zigzags, and one past a limit flies away; the fastest is in the middle.

claims.text: Gradient descent moves each step downhill by the step size times the slope: x ← x − η·f′(x).
claims.source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2016), §4.3 (gradient-based optimization).

claims.text: On the valley f(x) = x², the slope is 2x, so one step multiplies the position by (1 − 2η).
Starting at x = 4, ten steps with step size 0.05 or 0.95 both end about 1.39 from the bottom (one crawling, one zigzagging); with 0.45 the ball is within 0.04 of the bottom after two steps.
claims.source: Distance after n steps is |1 − 2η|^n · 4: 0.9^10 · 4 = 1.395 for η = 0.05 and η = 0.95; 0.1^2 · 4 = 0.04 for η = 0.45.

claims.text: On f(x) = x², any step size above 1 makes each step land farther from the bottom: at 1.05, ten steps from x = 4 end about 10.4 away.

Training real neural networks faces the same trade-off: too small a learning rate makes training slow, too large makes it oscillate or diverge, so the learning rate is often the most important setting to tune.
claims.source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (2016), §8.3.1 and §11.4.1 ("If you have time to tune only one hyperparameter, tune the learning rate").

claims.text: Neural networks are trained with variants of gradient descent that update all of their parameters at once, and those can number in the millions.
claims.source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (2016), §6.5 and §8.3 (stochastic gradient descent); network sizes in §1.2.3.

recall.question: Gradient descent is zigzagging back and forth across a valley and getting no closer. What should you change?
options: Take more steps with the same size
recall.why: Zigzagging means each step overshoots the bottom. A smaller step size stops the overshoot; a bigger one makes it worse.
